about.p: This course takes your phrasal verbs to an advanced level. You already know *give up* and *look after*; here you meet the verbs that make advanced English precise and lively – *stave off* a crisis, *gloss over* a problem, *flesh out* an argument, *rein in* spending. Many of them are common in journalism, academic writing and business, as well as in informal conversation.

Units 1–8 look at how phrasal verbs work: their grammar, the nouns and adjectives formed from them, collocation, register, metaphor and idioms. Units 9–15 explore the key particles, and units 16–55 present phrasal verbs by concept, function and topic – from memory and conflict to study, money, relationships, nature and the news. Units 56–60 focus on five key verbs: *come*, *get*, *go*, *keep* and *take*.

about.-: Each card gives a phrasal verb with its meaning and an example. Notes tell you when a verb is informal or formal, and when the object can go between the verb and the particle (*separable*).
*Complete the phrase* questions hide the particle and ask you to choose it.
Work through Units 1–4 first if you are not sure how phrasal verbs, phrasal nouns and phrasal adjectives behave.

about.tip: Notice what each verb typically goes with: you *stave off* a crisis or hunger, *rein in* spending, *flesh out* a plan. Record these partners with the verb.

units.sub: bring about, carry out, set in

L.p: A phrasal verb combines a verb with a particle (an adverb or preposition), or with two particles. The combination often means something quite different from the verb alone: *bring about* means cause, *carry out* means perform or complete, and bad weather *sets in* when it begins and seems likely to last. At advanced level you need to recognise these verbs even when an object separates the verb from its particle.

L.e: The new laws brought about a dramatic fall in pollution. Engineers carried out a full safety inspection. Winter has set in early this year. I've been meaning to sort all my old photos out for years.

L.p: Phrasal verbs are not only informal. Headlines and news reports use them constantly because they are short and vivid: prices *shoot up*, talks *break down*, a minister *steps down*. Academic and business writing uses many too: researchers *set out* to answer a question, and new figures *bear out* a theory (show that it is true).

L.e: Fuel prices have shot up again. Talks between the unions and management broke down last night. The chief executive is stepping down after twelve years. The study sets out to measure the effect of sleep on memory. The latest figures bear out our predictions.

L.x: The results *bear out* (not *bear up*) the theory.

L.p: Learn phrasal verbs in context, noting the words that typically go with them: you *carry out a threat*, research or an experiment; *panic sets in*; you *bring about change* or reform. Record whether a verb takes an object and whether it is formal or informal – and try to use it actively, not just understand it when you read.

L.e: The government has carried out its threat to raise taxes. As the hours passed, panic began to set in. Small steps can bring about lasting change.

units.t: Phrasal verbs: what they are and how they are used

units.sub: separable, inseparable, three-part verbs

L.h: A With and without an object

L.p: Some phrasal verbs are *intransitive* – they have no object: *The engine cut out*, *The scandal blew over*. Others are *transitive*: *They laid off forty staff*. Many can be both, with different meanings: *The idea took off* (became successful) but *He took off his jacket* (removed it).

L.e: The engine cut out halfway up the hill. The scandal soon blew over. The firm laid off forty staff. The idea took off immediately. He took off his jacket and sat down.

L.p: With *separable* verbs, a noun object can come before or after the particle (*sort out the problem* or *sort the problem out*), but a pronoun must come in the middle (*sort it out*). With *inseparable* verbs, the object always follows the particle: *I came across an old diary*; *We looked into it*. Long objects usually follow the particle: *He handed in a report that ran to forty pages*.

L.e: Somebody needs to sort the kitchen out. Somebody needs to sort out the kitchen. Please sort it out today. I came across some old photos. Police are looking into it. She handed in a report that ran to forty pages.

L.x: Here's the form – please *fill it in* (not *fill in it*).

L.p: Three-part verbs keep the object at the end: *I won't put up with this*, *She came up with a solution*. Some also take a second object: *They put the delay down to bad weather* (said it was caused by it). Transitive phrasal verbs can be passive: *The meeting was called off*; *The plan was put forward by a student*.

L.e: I won't put up with this noise any longer. She came up with a brilliant compromise. They put the delay down to bad weather. The meeting has been called off. The proposal was put forward by a first-year student.

units.sub: breakthrough, downturn, outlay

L.p: Many nouns are formed from phrasal verbs with the verb first: *a breakthrough* (an important discovery), *a cover-up* (an attempt to hide the truth), *a mix-up* (a confusing mistake), *a let-down* (a disappointment) and *turnout* (the number of people who attend or vote). Some are written as one word and some with a hyphen, so check a dictionary.

L.e: Scientists have made a breakthrough in the treatment of malaria. The inquiry found evidence of a cover-up. There was a mix-up over the hotel booking. The final episode was a real let-down. Turnout at the election was the lowest for decades.

L.x: There was a *mix-up* (not *mix-out*) with our tickets.

L.p: Other nouns put the particle first: *a downturn* (a fall in business activity), *an outlay* (money spent, especially at the start), *an outburst* (a sudden show of strong emotion), *upkeep* (the cost of maintaining something), *the outlook* (what is likely to happen) and *the onset* of something bad (its beginning).

L.e: The industry is suffering a downturn. Setting up the café required an initial outlay of £30,000. The minister apologised for his outburst. The upkeep of an old house can be very expensive. The economic outlook is uncertain. Doctors noticed the onset of symptoms early.

L.p: Phrasal nouns are very common in journalism and business, and they collocate strongly: *a dramatic breakthrough*, *a sharp downturn*, *a gloomy outlook*. Some have several uses: a *breakdown* can be a car that stops working, the failure of talks, or a person's mental collapse – *a nervous breakdown*.

L.e: Negotiators have made a dramatic breakthrough. The figures show a sharp downturn in sales. The company has a gloomy outlook for next year. He suffered a nervous breakdown after years of stress. There has been a breakdown in communication between the two departments.

units.sub: outspoken, rundown, worn out

L.p: Some adjectives put the particle first: *outspoken* (expressing opinions openly, even if they offend), *upcoming* (happening soon), *outgoing* (friendly and sociable – or leaving a job), *ongoing* (continuing), *overgrown* (covered with plants that have grown too much) and *uplifting* (making you feel happier).

L.e: She's an outspoken critic of the government. Tickets for the upcoming tour are on sale now. He's very outgoing and makes friends easily. The outgoing president gave a farewell speech. Negotiations are ongoing. The garden was completely overgrown. It's an uplifting film about hope and friendship.

L.p: Others put the verb first, often as a past participle: *rundown* (in poor condition, or tired and unwell), *worn out* (exhausted, or damaged by use), *broken-down* (not working), *cut off* (isolated) and *fed up* (bored and annoyed). Before a noun they usually take a hyphen: *a broken-down car*.

L.e: The hotel was rather rundown. I'm absolutely worn out after the move. A broken-down van was blocking the lane. The village feels very cut off in winter. I'm fed up with this weather.

L.x: A *broken-down* (not *broken*) lorry was blocking the road.

L.p: Some phrasal adjectives describe the effect something has: *off-putting* (unpleasant, making you not want something) and *forthcoming* (willing to give information, or about to happen). Others describe people's states: *laid-back* (relaxed), *hard-up* (short of money, informal) and *washed-out* (pale and tired).

L.e: The smell from the kitchen was rather off-putting. The minister was not very forthcoming about the plans. He's very laid-back about deadlines. We were pretty hard-up when we were students. You look washed-out – are you OK?

units.sub: doubts creep in, draw up a contract, rule out a possibility

L.p: Many phrasal verbs prefer particular subjects. *Doubts creep in* (begin gradually), *rumours go round*, *tension builds up*, *a storm blows up* (begins suddenly), *a dispute drags on*, and *the novelty wears off*. Learning the subject together with the verb makes your English sound natural.

L.e: After the first week, doubts began to creep in. Rumours are going round that the factory will close. Tension had been building up for months. A storm blew up while we were at sea. The legal dispute dragged on for years. When the novelty wore off, the children got bored.

L.x: Doubts began to *creep in* (not *creep on*) after the first week.

L.p: Other phrasal verbs prefer particular objects. You *draw up a contract*, a list or a plan; you *rule out a possibility*; you *call off a search* or a strike; you *lay down conditions* or rules; and you *iron out differences*. You *stave off* hunger, defeat or a crisis when you stop it happening for a while.

L.e: The lawyers drew up a new contract. Police have not ruled out the possibility of murder. The search was called off at nightfall. The agreement lays down strict conditions. The two sides met to iron out their differences. The loan helped the company stave off bankruptcy.

L.p: Phrasal verbs also have favourite adverbs: you *flatly turn down* an offer, *quietly slip away* from a party and *eventually come round* to a plan. You *badly let someone down* when you disappoint them very much.

L.e: She flatly turned down the offer. He quietly slipped away before the speeches. My parents eventually came round to the idea. I'm sorry – I've badly let you down.

units.sub: pass away, pop in, embark on

L.p: Some phrasal verbs belong to formal writing. You *embark on* a project (start it), *adhere to* rules (follow them), *abide by* a decision (accept and obey it), *dispense with* something unnecessary (stop using it) and *refrain from* doing something (not do it). Polite language uses *pass away* for die.

L.e: The council is embarking on a major housing programme. All members must adhere to the code of conduct. Both sides agreed to abide by the court's decision. Let's dispense with the formalities. Passengers are asked to refrain from smoking. Her grandmother passed away peacefully last night.

L.x: Both sides agreed to *abide by* (not *abide to*) the decision.

L.p: Many phrasal verbs are informal and belong in conversation: *pop in* (visit briefly), *suss out* (understand, British English), *mess up* (spoil, or do badly), *kick off* (start; in British English also become angry), *chuck out* (throw away) and *fob off* (persuade someone to accept less than they want).

L.e: Pop in for a coffee when you're passing. I couldn't suss out what was going on. I completely messed up my driving test. The meeting kicks off at nine. Fans kicked off when the referee gave a penalty. Don't let them fob you off with excuses.

L.p: In formal writing, a single verb is often better than a phrasal verb: *investigate* rather than *look into*, *postpone* rather than *put off*, *discover* rather than *find out*. But many phrasal verbs are neutral and fit any register, such as *carry out*, *set up*, *point out* and *take over*.

L.e: The committee will investigate the complaint, though in conversation we'd say we'll look into it. The meeting has been postponed – or, informally, we've put it off. The report points out several weaknesses. The company was taken over last year.

units.sub: iron out, mull over, brush up

L.p: Many phrasal verbs take a picture from everyday life and use it for ideas. You *iron out* problems (remove them, like creases from cloth), *brush up* a skill (refresh it, like dust from a coat), *patch up* a quarrel (repair it, perhaps only for a while) and *paper over* problems (hide them without solving them, like covering cracks in a wall).

L.e: We still need to iron out a few problems with the software. I must brush up my Spanish before the trip. They patched up their differences for the sake of the children. The government is trying to paper over the cracks.

L.x: We still need to *iron out* (not *iron off*) a few problems.

L.h: B Thinking as eating and cooking

L.p: Thinking is often described as eating or cooking. You *mull over* an idea (think about it carefully for some time) and *chew over* a problem (think about it slowly). You *cook up* a plan or an excuse when you invent it, often dishonestly. A long argument *boils down to* one point when that is its essence.

L.e: I'll mull it over and give you an answer tomorrow. We chewed over the problem for hours. He cooked up a story about losing his keys. The whole debate boils down to money.

L.p: A face *lights up* when it becomes happy, and an idea *dawns on* you when you suddenly realise it. A plan *gets off the ground* when it starts successfully. News or results *trickle in* when they arrive slowly, a little at a time.

L.e: Her face lit up when she saw the puppy. It suddenly dawned on me that I'd left my passport at home. The project never really got off the ground. Results are trickling in from rural areas.

units.sub: go off the rails, lay it on thick, fall by the wayside

L.p: Many idioms contain phrasal verbs. A person *goes off the rails* when they start behaving in a wild or unacceptable way. Informally, you *lay it on thick* when you exaggerate praise or feelings. You *let off steam* when you release strong feelings, and you *let your hair down* when you relax and enjoy yourself. Someone who *gets on your nerves* annoys you.

L.e: He went off the rails after his parents divorced. You're laying it on a bit thick, aren't you? The kids ran round the park to let off steam. It's the end of the exams – time to let our hair down! His constant humming really gets on my nerves.

L.x: He *went off the rails* (not *went off the roads*) as a teenager.

L.h: B Idioms about success and failure

L.p: Plans and people *fall by the wayside* when they fail or stop before the end. In British English, you *come up trumps* when you do better than expected. Something that *goes down a storm* is a great success. You *pull out all the stops* when you make every possible effort.

L.e: Many of the original applicants fell by the wayside. My little brother came up trumps with a brilliant present. Her speech went down a storm. We pulled out all the stops to finish on time.

L.p: Two people *get on like a house on fire* when they like each other very much. Something that *takes you down a peg or two* makes you less proud, and something that *brings you down to earth* makes you face reality. You *butter someone up* when you praise them because you want something.

L.e: The two grandmothers get on like a house on fire. Losing the final took him down a peg or two. The bill for the repairs soon brought us down to earth. He's buttering up the boss because he wants a pay rise.

units.sub: bandy about, fool around, hang about

L.p: *Around* and *about* often suggest activity without a clear purpose. You *fool around* or *mess about* when you behave in a silly way, *hang about* when you wait or spend time doing nothing in particular, and *lounge around* when you sit or lie in a lazy way. A person who *drifts around* moves from place to place without a plan.

L.e: Stop fooling around and help me carry these boxes. A group of teenagers were hanging about outside the station. We spent the whole Sunday lounging around in our pyjamas. After university he drifted around Europe for a couple of years.

L.p: Words and ideas can be *bandied about* – mentioned often, usually without much thought. Rumours *get about* (spread), and news *gets around*. People *throw* ideas *around* when they suggest them informally, and you *ask around* when you ask several people for information or help.

L.e: Figures like a million pounds were being bandied about in the press. It soon got about that the manager was leaving. We threw a few ideas around over coffee. I'll ask around and see if anyone knows a good plumber.

L.x: Big numbers are often *bandied about* (not *bandied around about*) in the press.

L.p: You *turn* a situation *around* when you change it from bad to good, and a company that improves dramatically has *a turnaround*. You *bring* someone *around* when you persuade them to agree, or when you make them conscious again. Something *comes about* when it happens, and you *go about* a task in a particular way.

L.e: The new manager turned the club around in a single season. It was a remarkable turnaround in the company's fortunes. She was against the idea at first, but we brought her around. How did this situation come about? How would you go about learning Japanese?

units.sub: clamp down, water down, track down

L.p: *Down* often means reducing. You *water down* a plan or a law when you make it weaker, and you *tone down* language when you make it less offensive. You *scale down* a project (make it smaller) and *wind down* an activity (gradually reduce it before stopping). Prices *come down*, and companies *bring down* costs.

L.e: The final version of the law was watered down. The comedian was asked to tone down his jokes. The festival has been scaled down because of the cost. The company is winding down its operations in Asia. The price of solar panels has come down sharply.

L.x: The proposals were *watered down* (not *watered off*) by the committee.

L.p: Authorities *clamp down on* or *crack down on* something when they act strongly to stop it. You *hold down* prices (keep them low) and *keep down* noise or costs. A government can *put down* a rebellion (stop it by force). You *turn down* an offer when you refuse it, and you *back down* when you stop insisting.

L.e: Police are clamping down on drivers who use their phones. The government has promised to hold down fuel prices. Please keep the noise down – the baby's asleep. The army put down the uprising within days. The council backed down after a public outcry.

L.p: You *track down* someone or something when you find them after a long search, and you *hunt down* a criminal. You *jot down* a quick note and *take down* someone's details. A system *goes down* when it stops working, and you *let someone down* when you disappoint them. A person *breaks down* when they lose control of their emotions.

L.e: It took me months to track down my old school friend. Police hunted down the escaped prisoners. Let me jot down your number. The bank's website went down this morning. I'm counting on you – don't let me down. She broke down when she heard the news.

units.sub: cave in, chip in, rein in

L.p: *In* can suggest collapsing or giving way. A roof *caves in* when it falls inwards, and a person *caves in* when they stop resisting and agree. You *give in* when you accept defeat, and you *give in to* pressure or temptation. A person who is exhausted is *done in* (British English, informal).

L.e: The roof of the old mill caved in during the storm. After weeks of protests, the government caved in. In the end I gave in and bought the children a puppy. Don't give in to pressure from your friends. After the hike we were completely done in.

L.x: The government finally *caved in* (not *caved down*) to the protesters.

L.p: You *chip in* when you contribute money or add a comment to a conversation. You *pitch in* when you join others in helping with work, and you *join in* an activity. You *weigh in* when you join an argument with your opinion. You *fit in* when you are accepted by a group.

L.e: We all chipped in to buy her a leaving present. Can I chip in here? I think there's another option. Everyone pitched in to clear up after the party. The prime minister has weighed in on the debate. It took him a while to fit in at his new school.

L.p: You *rein in* spending or an emotion when you control it more strictly. A difficult situation can *hem you in* (limit your freedom), and you can be *boxed in* or *penned in* by rules or people. You *rope someone in* (informal) when you persuade them to help, and you *pull in* money or crowds when you attract them.

L.e: The government must rein in public spending. He felt hemmed in by all the rules at work. I got roped in to organising the school fair. The concert pulled in a crowd of 50,000.

units.sub: fend off, stave off, round off

L.p: *Off* often suggests keeping something away. You *fend off* an attack, questions or a rival (defend yourself against them), *stave off* a crisis or hunger (stop it for a while) and *ward off* illness or danger (prevent it). You *head off* a problem when you stop it before it happens, and you *see off* a challenge when you defeat it.

L.e: The minister fended off awkward questions from reporters. A quick snack will stave off hunger until dinner. Some people believe garlic wards off colds. Talks were held to head off a strike. The champion saw off a strong challenge from the young player.

L.x: A snack will *stave off* (not *stave away*) your hunger until dinner.

L.p: You *round off* an event or a meal when you end it in a satisfying way, and you *finish off* a task or food. You *polish off* food (informal, eat it all) and *write off* a debt (accept that it won't be paid). Companies *sell off* parts of the business, and they *lay off* staff when there is not enough work.

L.e: We rounded off the evening with a walk by the river. Let me just finish off this paragraph. The children polished off a whole cake. The bank has written off the loan. The group is selling off its hotels.

L.h: C Starting and setting in motion

L.p: *Off* can also mean starting. An event *kicks off* (begins), a joke or a remark *sets off* laughter, and a match or an argument *sparks off* trouble. Something *goes off* when it explodes or rings, and plans *come off* (succeed). You *pull off* something difficult when you manage it.

L.e: The festival kicks off with a parade on Friday. His remark set off a wave of laughter. The arrest sparked off two nights of rioting. A car alarm went off at three a.m. It was a risky plan, but it came off. Nobody thought they could pull it off.

units.sub: egg on, dote on, press on

L.p: *On* often means continuing. You *press on* with a task despite difficulties and *soldier on* when you continue bravely through problems. In British English, you *plough on* when you continue with something slow or boring. Someone who *rambles on* talks for too long in a confused way, and a dispute *rumbles on* when it continues without being settled.

L.e: Despite the rain, we pressed on to the summit. She had a cold but soldiered on through the conference. I ploughed on through the report until midnight. The speaker rambled on for over an hour. The row over the new airport rumbles on.

L.x: She had flu but *soldiered on* (not *soldiered away*) until the end of term.

L.p: You *egg someone on* when you encourage them, usually to do something silly or dangerous, and you *spur someone on* when you encourage them to try harder. You *dote on* someone when you love them very much, perhaps too much. Success can *hinge on* one factor (depend on it completely), and informally you *bank on* something when you rely on it.

L.e: His friends egged him on to climb the fence. The thought of the prize spurred her on. Grandad dotes on his only granddaughter. Whether the picnic goes ahead hinges on the weather. Don't bank on getting a pay rise this year.

L.h: C Taking on and turning on

L.p: You *take on* an opponent when you compete or fight against them. An idea *catches on* when it becomes popular. A dog *turns on* someone when it suddenly attacks them, and a group *rounds on* someone when it suddenly attacks them with words.

L.e: The small shop took on the supermarket giants and won. The idea never really caught on. The dog suddenly turned on its owner. When I criticised the plan, the whole team rounded on me.

units.sub: eke out, single out, phase out

L.p: *Out* can mean making something last as long as possible. You *eke out* a small amount of food or money (make it last), *spin out* a task (make it last longer than necessary) and *drag out* a process. You *ride out* a storm or a crisis when you survive it without serious damage.

L.e: Pensioners are eking out their savings as prices rise. He spun out his speech to fill the time. The lawyers dragged out the case for years. The company rode out the recession better than its rivals.

L.x: They *eked out* (not *eked up*) their supplies until help arrived.

L.p: You *single out* someone when you choose them for special praise or criticism, and you *pick out* something when you choose or recognise it in a group. You *weed out* unsuitable people or things (remove them), *rule out* a possibility and *opt out* of a scheme (choose not to take part).

L.e: The teacher singled her out for praise. Can you pick out your brother in this photo? The first interview is designed to weed out weak candidates. Police have ruled out foul play. You can opt out of the pension scheme if you wish.

L.p: Governments *phase out* a product or system (stop it gradually) and try to *stamp out* a problem (end it completely). A custom *dies out*, and people *burn out* when they become exhausted from working too hard. A detail *stands out* when it is easy to notice.

L.e: Coal power is being phased out across Europe. The new law aims to stamp out bullying. The custom has almost died out. Many nurses burn out after years of night shifts. One mistake stood out in the report.

units.sub: drum up, conjure up, prop up

L.p: *Up* often suggests creating or producing. You *drum up* support or business (get it by making an effort), *conjure up* an image or a memory (create it as if by magic) and *dream up* a plan (invent it, often an unusual one). A speaker can *whip up* a crowd's feelings, and tears or emotions *well up* inside you.

L.e: The band toured local radio stations to drum up support. The smell of baking conjured up memories of my grandmother's kitchen. Who dreamt up this crazy idea? The speaker whipped up the crowd into a frenzy. Tears welled up in her eyes.

L.x: They're trying to *drum up* (not *drum out*) support for the campaign.

L.p: You *prop up* something weak (support it to stop it falling or failing) and *shore up* a building or a position (strengthen it). You *back up* a claim with evidence, and an economy or a person *holds up* when they stay strong under pressure.

L.e: The government spent billions propping up the banks. Engineers shored up the old bridge. Can you back up that claim? The economy has held up well despite the crisis.

L.p: You *step up* efforts when you increase them, and factories *ramp up* production. A story that doesn't *add up* is not believable. *Up* can also mean completing: you *wrap up* a meeting and *tie up loose ends* (deal with the final details).

L.e: Police have stepped up patrols in the area. The factory is ramping up production. His story just doesn't add up. Let's wrap up the meeting. Before I leave, I need to tie up a few loose ends.

units.sub: while away, drag out, run on

L.p: You *while away* the hours when you spend time pleasantly with nothing to do. Time *drags on* when it passes slowly and *flies by* when it passes quickly. As an evening *wears on*, it gets later and later, and a meeting *runs on* when it continues longer than planned.

L.e: We whiled away the afternoon playing chess. The last hour of the flight dragged on. The summer flew by. As the evening wore on, the guests grew tired. The meeting ran on until nearly eight.

L.x: The meeting *ran on* (not *ran in*) until eight o'clock.

L.p: You *hold off* doing something when you delay it, and you *drag out* a process when you make it last longer than necessary. A project *falls behind* when it is later than planned. An event is *brought forward* when it is moved to an earlier time and *put back* when it is moved later.

L.e: We're holding off buying a car until prices fall. The lawyers dragged out the negotiations. The project has fallen behind schedule. The meeting has been brought forward to Monday. The launch has been put back a month.

L.p: Some things *date back to* a particular time. A friendship *goes back* a number of years. Music and memories *live on* (continue to exist), and a smell *lingers on*. Bad habits *catch up with* you when their effects finally reach you, and you *move on* when you stop thinking about the past.

L.e: The castle dates back to the eleventh century. Their friendship goes back thirty years. His music lives on long after his death. The smell of smoke lingered on for days. All those late nights eventually caught up with him. It's time to move on.

units.sub: bring on, set off, stem from

L.p: Several phrasal verbs mean cause. Something *brings on* an illness or an attack when it makes it start. An event *sets off* a reaction, *sparks off* trouble or *triggers off* a crisis. In formal English, a situation *gives rise to* problems or concern.

L.e: Lack of sleep can bring on a migraine. The news set off a wave of panic buying. The shooting sparked off riots across the city. A small error triggered off a major power cut. The new policy has given rise to widespread concern.

L.x: Cold weather can *bring on* (not *bring up*) an asthma attack.

L.p: To explain where something comes from, you can say it *stems from*, *arises from* (formal) or *springs from* a cause. You *put* something *down to* a cause when you say that is the reason for it, and you *trace* something *back to* its origin.

L.e: Many of his anxieties stem from his childhood. The dispute arose from a misunderstanding. Her interest in science sprang from a visit to a museum. I put my success down to hard work. The outbreak was traced back to a single restaurant.

L.p: One thing *leads to* another. Effects *spill over* into other areas, and one person's attitude can *rub off on* others. Hard work *pays off* when it brings success, but a plan can also *rebound on* the person who made it – harm them instead of the intended target.

L.e: Poor diet can lead to serious health problems. The strike has spilled over into other industries. Her enthusiasm rubbed off on the whole team. All that extra training paid off. His attempt to embarrass his rival rebounded on him.

units.sub: call up, come flooding back, blank out

L.p: Memories can *come flooding back* – return suddenly and in large numbers. A smell or a song can *bring back* memories or *call up* images of the past. You *look back on* earlier periods of your life, and you *think back to* a particular moment when you try to remember it.

L.e: When I saw the school again, the memories came flooding back. That song brings back my first year at university. The smell of pine calls up images of childhood holidays. Looking back on it, I was very lucky. Think back to the night of the party – who was there?

L.x: When I saw the house, memories *came flooding back* (not *came flowing back*).

L.p: You *blank out* a painful memory when you deliberately forget it, and you *blot out* unpleasant thoughts when you stop yourself thinking about them. A memory *fades away* over time, and a task *slips your mind* when you forget to do it.

L.e: She has blanked out most of the accident. Over the years, the memories faded away. Sorry – your birthday completely slipped my mind. He tried to blot out the memory of the war.

L.p: You *learn* something *off by heart* when you memorise it exactly, and in informal British English you *swot up on* facts before an exam. A photo or a question can *jog someone's memory*. A remark *sticks in your mind* when you remember it easily, and you *brush up on* knowledge you have partly forgotten.

L.e: We had to learn the poem off by heart. I'm swotting up on dates for my history exam. Perhaps this photo will jog your memory. One thing she said has stuck in my mind ever since. I need to brush up on my German before the trip.

units.sub: forge ahead, press on, fall behind

L.p: You *forge ahead* or *press ahead* when you make strong progress, especially despite difficulties. Work *gets under way* when it starts. You *build on* earlier success when you use it as a base for more, and business *picks up* when it improves after a slow period.

L.e: The company is forging ahead with its expansion plans. The council is pressing ahead with the new road despite protests. Work on the bridge got under way last spring. We need to build on this success. Business usually picks up after Christmas.

L.x: They are *forging ahead* (not *forging forward*) with their plans.

L.p: Progress can *grind to a halt* – slowly stop completely. A region *lags behind* others when it develops more slowly. Fear or a lack of money can *hold you back* (stop you progressing), and you *get bogged down* in details when they stop you moving forward.

L.e: Talks have ground to a halt. Our region lags behind the rest of the country. Lack of confidence held her back for years. We got bogged down in legal details.

L.h: C Catching up and breaking through

L.p: You *catch up* with others when you reach their level, and you *keep up* when you stay at it. A government *pushes through* reforms when it makes them happen despite opposition. A runner *pulls ahead* when she starts to lead, and negotiators *edge forward* when they make slow, careful progress.

L.e: After months of extra lessons, she caught up with the rest of the class. It's hard to keep up with all the changes. The government pushed through the reforms. In the final lap, the Kenyan pulled ahead. Negotiators edged forward towards an agreement.

units.sub: flare up, lash out, set upon

L.p: Violence *flares up* (starts suddenly) and fighting *breaks out* (begins). A small quarrel can *blow up* into a major row. People *square up to* each other when they prepare to fight, and a crowd *turns on* someone when it suddenly attacks them.

L.e: Violence flared up again after the funeral. Fighting broke out between rival gangs. A minor disagreement blew up into a full-scale row. The two players squared up to each other on the pitch. The crowd suddenly turned on the police.

L.x: Fighting *broke out* (not *broke off*) in the north of the country.

L.p: You *lash out* when you suddenly attack someone with blows or words. A gang *sets upon* a victim (attacks them violently), and attackers *beat up* someone (hit them repeatedly, informal). Informally, you *lay into* someone when you attack them physically or with criticism. Troops *close in on* a target when they gradually surround it.

L.e: When I tried to help, he lashed out at me. The tourist was set upon by a gang of youths. The victim was badly beaten up. She laid into her brother for losing the keys. Troops closed in on the rebel stronghold.

L.p: Fighting *dies down* when it becomes less intense, and protests *peter out* when they gradually end. Rebels *lay down their arms* when they stop fighting. Police *break up* a fight, and troops are *stood down* when they are no longer needed.

L.e: The fighting died down after midnight. The protests gradually petered out. The rebels agreed to lay down their arms. Police broke up the fight outside the pub. The troops were stood down after the ceasefire.

units.sub: blare out, ring out, drown out

L.p: Loud music *blares out*, and a shot or a voice *rings out* (is heard loudly and clearly). One noise *drowns out* another when it covers it so that it can't be heard. Someone *pipes up* when they suddenly speak, especially in a small voice, and a crowd *shouts down* a speaker when it shouts so that the speaker can't be heard.

L.e: Pop music blared out from every shop. A single shot rang out across the valley. The noise of the traffic drowned out our conversation. A little girl at the back piped up with a question. Protesters shouted down the minister.

L.x: The traffic *drowned out* (not *drowned down*) our voices.

L.p: Sounds *die away* when they become quieter until they stop, and a song *fades out* at the end. Conversation *tails off* when it becomes quieter and stops, and a speaker *trails off* when they stop gradually without finishing. You *keep* your voice *down* when you speak quietly.

L.e: The sound of the engine died away in the distance. The song fades out at the end. Her voice tailed off as the teacher walked in. He trailed off, unsure how to finish. Keep your voice down – the baby's asleep.

L.p: Machines *start up* with a noise and then *hum away* in the background. An old engine *splutters out* when it stops after a series of uneven sounds. Alarms *go off* when they ring loudly.

L.e: The generator started up with a roar. The fridge hummed away in the corner. The old engine spluttered out halfway up the hill. A car alarm went off in the street below.

units.sub: stand by, side with, come out against

L.p: You *stand by* someone when you support them in difficulty, and informally you *stick up for* them when you defend them. You *side with* someone in an argument. Friends *rally round* a person who needs help. You *come out in favour of* a plan when you publicly support it.

L.e: Her family stood by her throughout the trial. My brother always stuck up for me at school. Most of the committee sided with the chairman. Friends rallied round when she lost her job. The newspaper came out in favour of the new law.

L.x: Most members *sided with* (not *sided to*) the chairman.

L.p: You *come out against* a plan when you publicly oppose it, and you *speak out against* injustice. You *stand up to* a powerful person when you refuse to be treated badly by them, and you *hold out against* pressure when you continue to resist it. People *turn against* someone they used to support.

L.e: Several MPs have come out against the proposal. She spoke out against discrimination in the workplace. It takes courage to stand up to a bully. The workers held out against the new contracts for months. Public opinion has turned against the government.

L.p: People *go over to* the other side when they change their support, and they *come round to* a view when they start to accept it. Support *falls away* when it becomes less. You *win* people *over* when you persuade them to support you, and voters *swing behind* a candidate when they start to support them.

L.e: Several of his supporters have gone over to the opposition. My father has come round to the idea of an electric car. Support for the party has fallen away. She won the audience over with her honesty. Voters have swung behind the new leader.

units.sub: go along with, fall in with, come round to

L.h: A Agreeing with people and plans

L.p: You *go along with* a plan or a person when you agree, often without enthusiasm, and you *fall in with* someone's plans when you accept them. Two people *see eye to eye* when they agree. Countries *sign up to* an agreement when they formally accept it, and informally you *buy into* an idea when you believe in it.

L.e: I didn't like the plan, but I went along with it. We fell in with their plans for the weekend. My sister and I rarely see eye to eye. All the member states signed up to the agreement. Not everyone has bought into the new strategy.

L.x: I didn't like the idea, but I *went along with* (not *went along to*) it.

L.p: You *come round to* someone's point of view after first disagreeing. You *settle on* a choice after discussion. Negotiators *hammer out* or *thrash out* a deal when they agree it after long, difficult discussion. You *meet someone halfway* when you compromise.

L.e: My grandmother hated mobile phones at first, but she has come round to them. After hours of debate, we settled on a date. The two sides hammered out a deal in the early hours. Let's thrash out the details tomorrow. If you lower the price a little, I'll meet you halfway.

L.p: In a discussion, you *chime in with* a comment, often to agree with what someone has said. Facts *bear out* a statement when they show it is true. One account *squares with* another when they match, and new findings *tie in with* earlier research when they agree with it.

L.e: Several others chimed in with similar complaints. The figures bear out what she told us. His story doesn't square with the evidence. The new findings tie in with earlier research.

units.sub: cotton on, hit upon, latch on

L.p: Informally, you *cotton on* (British English) when you begin to understand something, and you *latch on* when you understand an idea and start to use it. You *figure out* a problem when you solve it, and you *make out* what someone means when you manage to understand it. You *get* your ideas *across* when you make others understand them.

L.e: It took me ages to cotton on to what was happening. The children latched on to the rules very quickly. I can't figure out how this machine works. I can't make out what he's trying to say. She gets her ideas across very clearly.

L.x: It took me a while to *cotton on* (not *cotton up*) to the joke.

L.p: You *hit upon* an idea when you suddenly think of it, and you *come up with* a plan or a solution. You *dream up* an unusual idea and *think up* an excuse or a name. An idea *dawns on* you when you gradually realise it.

L.e: Then we hit upon the idea of selling cakes. Engineers have come up with a cheaper design. Who dreamt up this ridiculous scheme? We need to think up a name for the shop. It gradually dawned on me that I'd been tricked.

L.p: You *think through* a plan when you consider every part of it, and you *turn over* an idea in your mind. You *weigh up* the options when you compare advantages and disadvantages. You *sound out* someone when you discover their opinion informally, and you *bounce* ideas *off* colleagues when you discuss them to test them.

L.e: The plan hasn't been properly thought through. I've been turning the idea over in my mind all week. We need to weigh up the costs and benefits. Can you sound out the staff before we decide? I like to bounce ideas off my colleagues.

units.sub: set up, line up, pencil in

L.p: You *set up* a meeting or an event (arrange it), and you *line up* speakers or performers (arrange for them to take part). You *lay on* food or transport (provide it, British English), *sort out* the details and *firm up* plans when you make them definite. You *pencil in* a date when you arrange it provisionally.

L.e: I've set up a meeting with the bank for Thursday. The festival has lined up some great bands this year. The hotel laid on a minibus from the station. Let's firm up the arrangements next week. I'll pencil in the 14th, but I'll need to confirm.

L.x: I'll *pencil in* (not *pen in*) Friday, but it may change.

L.p: You *bring forward* an event when you move it earlier and *put back* (or *push back*) an event when you move it later. You *call off* something when you cancel it, and you *rearrange* or *reschedule* it. You *fit* someone *in* when you find time to see them, and you *squeeze in* an extra activity in a busy day.

L.e: The match has been brought forward to Saturday. The launch has been pushed back until the spring. The concert was called off because of the storm. The dentist can fit you in on Friday morning. I managed to squeeze in a quick swim before work.

L.p: You *see to* a task when you deal with it, and you *follow up* an enquiry when you take further action. You *chase up* someone or something when you remind them about a task that hasn't been done. You *tie up* the loose ends at the end of a project, and you *iron out* any problems before the event.

L.e: Don't worry about the tickets – I'll see to them. I'll follow up your enquiry with the manager. Could you chase up the printers about our posters? We need to tie up a few loose ends before the launch. We ironed out the last problems at the rehearsal.

units.sub: add up to, tot up, bump up

L.p: You *add up* numbers (calculate the total), and numbers *add up to* a total. Informally, you *tot up* (British English) a bill or your points. You *work out* a sum and *count up* the votes. Something that *comes to* a figure reaches that total, and costs that *run into* thousands reach that level.

L.e: Can you add up these figures for me? The bill added up to more than £300. Let's tot up the scores. The votes are still being counted up. The repairs came to £450. The cost of the damage could run into millions.

L.x: The bill *came to* (not *came up*) almost £200.

L.p: Informally, you *bump up* prices or numbers when you increase them. Costs *mount up* and debts *pile up* when they increase gradually. Businesses *scale up* production (make it bigger) and *step up* efforts. Prices *shoot up* or *soar*, and a company *boosts* sales or *beefs up* security (makes it stronger, informal).

L.e: The hotel bumps up its prices in August. Small costs soon mount up. The company is scaling up production to meet demand. Security has been beefed up at the airport. Fuel prices shot up overnight.

L.p: You *cut down on* spending or salt, *cut back* when you reduce costs, and *whittle down* a list (reduce it gradually). You *pare down* (or *pare back*) something to its essentials. Figures *go down*, and enthusiasm *tails off*. A company *scales back* its plans when it makes them smaller.

L.e: We need to cut back on travel this year. We whittled the list of candidates down to three. The designer pared the collection down to ten pieces. Sales tailed off after Christmas. The airline has scaled back its expansion plans.

units.sub: pull off, bomb out, fizzle out

L.p: You *pull off* something difficult when you manage to do it, and a plan *comes off* when it succeeds. Informally, you *make it* when you become successful. A product *takes off* when it suddenly becomes popular, and effort *pays off* when it brings success. You *come through* a difficult test when you pass it, and you *sail through* an exam when you pass it easily.

L.e: Nobody thought the small club could pull off a win. The surprise party came off perfectly. After years of struggling, the band finally made it. Electric bikes have really taken off. All her hard work paid off. She sailed through her final exams.

L.x: It was risky, but they *pulled it off* (not *pulled it up*).

L.p: Plans *fall through* when they don't happen, and projects *fall apart* when they collapse. Enthusiasm or a campaign *fizzles out* (ends weakly, without result), and something *peters out* (gradually ends). Informally, a performer *bombs* or a student *bombs out* when they fail badly. A business *goes under* (fails), and a person *flunks* an exam (American English, informal).

L.e: The sale of our flat fell through when the buyer's mortgage was refused. The coalition fell apart after six months. The protest fizzled out after a few days. The path petered out in the middle of the woods. Their new show bombed. Many small businesses went under during the crisis.

L.p: After failure, you *bounce back* (recover quickly) or *pick yourself up* and start again. You *come back* when you return to success, and a team *pulls back* a goal (reduces the other team's lead). You *turn* a situation *around* when you change it from failure to success.

L.e: After losing her job, she bounced back with a new business. He picked himself up and tried again. The singer has come back with a brilliant new album. United pulled back a goal just before half-time. The new coach turned the team around in a season.

units.sub: iron out, gloss over, grapple with

L.p: Problems *crop up* or *come up* (appear unexpectedly), and difficulties *build up* (increase gradually). A situation *gets out of hand* when it can no longer be controlled. You *come up against* opposition or obstacles (meet them), and you *run into* trouble when you start to have it.

L.e: A few problems have cropped up with the new system. Complaints had been building up for months. The situation at the border is getting out of hand. The plan came up against fierce opposition. The project ran into trouble almost immediately.

L.x: The plan *came up against* (not *came up to*) fierce opposition.

L.p: You *grapple with* a problem (try hard to deal with it), *get to grips with* it (start to understand and deal with it) and *face up to* it (accept it exists). You *iron out* small problems and *sort out* bigger ones. You *get round* a problem (find a way to avoid it), and you *thrash out* a solution through discussion.

L.e: The government is still grappling with high inflation. It took me weeks to get to grips with the new software. Sooner or later he'll have to face up to his drinking problem. We should be able to iron out these difficulties. We got round the problem by changing suppliers.

L.p: You *gloss over* a problem when you treat it as less important than it is, and you *skate over* a subject when you mention it very briefly to avoid it. You *paper over* problems when you hide them without solving them. You *shy away from* a difficult decision (avoid it because you are nervous), and you *put off* dealing with something unpleasant.

L.e: The report glosses over the company's financial problems. He skated over the subject of his previous job. The agreement merely papered over the cracks. Politicians often shy away from unpopular decisions. I keep putting off phoning the bank.

units.sub: plump for, hinge on, talk round

L.p: You *opt for* one choice, or in informal British English you *plump for* it. You *settle on* one option out of several, and a committee *comes down in favour of* one side when it finally chooses it. A decision can *hinge on* one factor (depend on it completely). You *sleep on* a decision when you wait until the next day to make it.

L.e: In the end I plumped for the green sofa. We opted for a quiet wedding. After much discussion, they settled on a name for the baby. The panel came down in favour of the cheaper design. The whole decision hinges on the cost. Don't decide now – sleep on it.

L.x: In the end we *plumped for* (not *plumped on*) the blue one.

L.p: You *talk someone round* when you persuade them to change their mind, and you *talk someone out of* a plan when you persuade them not to do it. A good speech can *win over* doubtful listeners. You *bring* a group *round* to your view, and informally you *lean on* someone when you put pressure on them.

L.e: Dad was against the trip, but Mum talked him round. She talked me out of selling the house. The speech won over the undecided voters. We managed to bring the committee round. The company leaned on its suppliers to cut prices.

L.h: C Changing your mind – or not

L.p: You *go back on* a decision or promise when you change it, and you *back out of* an arrangement when you withdraw. You *have second thoughts* when you start to doubt a decision. You *stick to* a decision when you don't change it, and you *see* a difficult plan *through* when you continue until it is finished.

L.e: The government has gone back on its promise. Two investors backed out of the deal. I'm having second thoughts about the job. We've decided, so let's stick to it. It won't be easy, but we'll see it through.

units.sub: watch it, steady on, back off

L.p: Some short phrases are used as warnings: *Look out!* warns of danger, and in British English *Mind out!* means move or be careful. *Watch it!* is a warning to be careful, often said angrily. You tell someone to *watch out for* a particular danger, and to *keep away from* something dangerous.

L.e: Look out! There's a bus coming! Mind out – the floor's wet. Watch it! You nearly hit me with that bag. Watch out for pickpockets in the market. Keep away from the edge of the cliff.

L.x: *Watch it!* (not *See it!*) You nearly knocked me over.

L.p: In informal British English, *Steady on!* tells someone that what they are saying or doing is too extreme. *Cool it!* tells people to calm down. *Back off!* tells someone to stop threatening or criticising you, and *Lay off!* means stop criticising or annoying someone. In British English, *Pack it in!* means stop doing that.

L.e: Steady on – there's no need to shout at him. Cool it, both of you! Back off – this has nothing to do with you. Lay off him – he's had a tough week. Pack it in, you two, or there'll be no pudding!

L.p: *Come on!* encourages someone to hurry or try harder, and *Go on!* encourages someone to do something they are unsure about. *Hang on!* asks someone to wait. *Out with it!* tells someone to say what they are hiding, and *Keep at it!* means don't stop trying.

L.e: Come on – you can do it! Go on, try a bit – it's delicious. Hang on, I'm just coming. Come on, out with it! What's wrong? Keep at it – you're improving every day.

units.sub: slog away, plough through, farm out

L.p: Informally, you *slog away* at something when you work hard on it for a long time, and you *plough through* a large amount of work when you deal with it slowly and with effort. You *knuckle down* when you start working seriously. In British English, you *beaver away* when you work hard and steadily, and you *get stuck into* a job when you start it with energy.

L.e: She's been slogging away at her thesis for months. I ploughed through two hundred emails this morning. It's time to knuckle down and revise. He's been beavering away in the garden all day. Once we got stuck into the painting, we finished quickly.

L.x: I *ploughed through* (not *ploughed over*) all the paperwork.

L.p: Companies *farm out* or *contract out* work when they give it to people outside the organisation. You *take on* extra work when you agree to do it, and you *pass on* information to colleagues. You *fill in for* someone when you do their job while they are away.

L.e: The company farms out most of its design work to freelancers. Cleaning has been contracted out to a private firm. I've taken on two new projects this month. Can you pass on the message to the team? I'm filling in for the manager while she's on holiday.

L.p: You *start out* in a junior job and *work your way up* through a company. You *move on* when you leave for a new job, and you *stand down* when you leave an important position. You *put in for* a transfer or promotion when you apply for it.

L.e: She started out as a secretary and is now a director. He worked his way up from the post room. After five years, I was ready to move on. The chairman is standing down next year. I've put in for a transfer to Edinburgh.

units.sub: swot up, bone up on, mug up

L.p: Before exams, British students *swot up on* a subject (study it hard) or *mug up on* facts (learn them quickly). Informally, you *bone up on* a topic when you study it in detail. You *go over* your notes and *read up on* background material.

L.e: I spent the weekend swotting up on European history. He mugged up on the main dates the night before. Bone up on the company before your interview. Go over your notes the evening before the exam. I need to read up on the causes of the war.

L.x: I need to *read up on* (not *read on*) the topic before the seminar.

L.p: You *take in* information when you understand and remember it, and you *pick up* skills without formal study. Informally, you *get the hang of* a technique when you learn how to do it. You *fall behind* when you don't keep up, and you *catch up on* work you have missed.

L.e: The lecture was so fast that I couldn't take it all in. She picked up Italian while working in Milan. Once you get the hang of it, it's easy. I fell behind after missing a week of classes. I need to catch up on my reading.

L.p: You *sign up for* a course, and you *drop out* when you leave before finishing. You *sail through* an exam when you pass it easily and *scrape through* when you only just pass. Work with mistakes, or work handed in late, is *marked down*.

L.e: I've signed up for an online course in coding. He dropped out of university in his second year. She sailed through her finals. I only just scraped through statistics. My essay was marked down for being late.

units.sub: touch on, expand on, wrap up

L.p: A lecturer *sets out* the aims of a talk (explains them clearly) and *runs through* the main points (goes over them quickly). They *touch on* a topic when they mention it briefly and *expand on* an idea when they give more detail. They may *come back to* a point later, and at the end they *wrap up* the session.

L.e: In her introduction, she set out the three aims of the course. Let me just run through the main points again. I'll touch on this briefly now and come back to it next week. Could you expand on what you said about climate data? Let's wrap up there for today.

L.x: I'll *touch on* (not *touch at*) this topic briefly today.

L.p: Students *put forward* ideas and *bring up* questions. You *pick up on* a point someone made when you return to it to discuss it further, and you speak *following on from* another speaker. You *draw on* your reading when you use it as a source.

L.e: She put forward an interesting theory about the data. Ana brought up a good question about funding. I'd like to pick up on what Tom said earlier. Following on from that point, I think we should look at the costs. Draw on examples from the reading list.

L.p: You *jot down* notes during a lecture and *write* them *up* afterwards. If a lecturer speaks too fast, you can't *keep up*. Informally, listeners *switch off* when they stop paying attention.

L.e: I jotted down the key references. I always write up my notes the same evening. The lecturer spoke so fast I couldn't keep up. By the end, half the room had switched off.

units.sub: flesh out, set out, back up

L.p: Before writing, you *map out* the structure of an essay and *jot down* ideas. You *narrow down* a topic when you make it more focused, and you *draw up* an outline. Then you *flesh out* the outline – add details to turn it into a full draft.

L.e: Map out your essay before you start writing. I jotted down everything I could think of. You need to narrow down your topic – it's far too broad. I drew up an outline with five sections. Now flesh out each section with examples.

L.x: You need to *narrow down* (not *narrow up*) your topic.

L.p: You *set out* your argument clearly and *back up* each claim with sources. You *point out* weaknesses in other arguments, and you *build on* earlier research when you develop it further. You *weigh up* the evidence on both sides before you reach a conclusion.

L.e: The introduction should set out your main argument. Back up every claim with a reliable source. She pointed out a flaw in the original study. This essay builds on earlier work by Smith. After weighing up the evidence, I came down on the side of reform.

L.p: You *read through* a draft carefully, *cut out* repetition and *tighten up* loose sentences (make them more concise). You *tidy up* the references and *round off* the essay with a strong conclusion before you hand it in.

L.e: Read through your draft aloud to check it flows. Cut out any repetition. Tighten up your introduction – it's too long. Tidy up the references before you submit. Round off the essay with a clear conclusion.

units.sub: buy into, float off, wind up

L.p: Entrepreneurs *set up* companies, and a successful firm *branches out* into new areas. Investors *buy into* a company when they buy shares in it, and one owner *buys out* another. A group can *float off* or *spin off* part of its business as a separate company.

L.e: She set up her first company at twenty-two. The firm has branched out into renewable energy. A Japanese bank has bought into the company. The founders were bought out by a larger group. The group plans to float off its online division. The university spun off a small biotech firm.

L.x: The firm has *branched out* (not *branched away*) into renewable energy.

L.p: Negotiators *hammer out* a deal through long discussion. A deal *goes through* when it is completed, or *falls through* when it fails. A buyer *pulls out* when they withdraw, and companies *put in a bid* when they make an offer.

L.e: The two firms hammered out a deal over the weekend. The merger finally went through in March. A rival bid for the factory fell through when the bank refused a loan. The investors pulled out after seeing the accounts. They put in a bid of £5 million.

L.p: In hard times, companies *cut back on* spending and *sell off* assets. A business *goes under* when it fails, and it is *wound up* when it is officially closed. A struggling bank may be *bailed out* with government money.

L.e: The airline has cut back on routes and laid off staff. The group sold off its overseas hotels. Many small retailers went under during the recession. The company was wound up last year. The bank was bailed out with public money.

units.sub: rake in, fork out, eke out

L.p: Informally, a business *rakes in* money when it earns a lot easily, and a person *pulls in* a good salary. You *come into* money when you inherit it. You *put by* money for the future, and you *dip into* your savings when you use some of them.

L.e: The festival rakes in millions every summer. She pulls in about £80,000 a year. He came into a fortune when his aunt died. I put by a little every month. We had to dip into our savings to pay for the repairs.

L.x: He *came into* (not *came across*) a fortune when his aunt died.

L.p: Informally, you *fork out* or *shell out* money when you pay a lot, often unwillingly. In British English, you *splash out* when you spend a lot on something special. You *run up* debts when you let them grow, and informally you *blow* money when you spend it carelessly.

L.e: We had to fork out £600 for a new boiler. I shelled out a fortune for these tickets. We splashed out on a meal at a famous restaurant. He ran up huge debts on his credit cards. She blew all her savings on a world trip.

L.p: You *eke out* a small amount of money when you make it last, and you *get by* or *scrape by* on a low income. You *tighten your belt* when you spend less. When you *pay off* a debt or a mortgage, you pay all of it.

L.e: Pensioners are eking out their savings. Students often get by on very little. We scraped by on my part-time wages. With prices rising, we'll all have to tighten our belts. It took us twenty years to pay off the mortgage.

units.sub: do up, knock through, clear out

L.p: You *do up* a house when you repair and decorate it, and you *knock through* when you remove a wall to join two rooms. You *put up* shelves, and empty buildings are *boarded up* when their windows are covered with wooden boards. Informally, you *spruce up* a room when you make it look neater and more attractive.

L.e: They bought a ruined cottage and did it up. We knocked through to make one big kitchen. My dad put up the shelves in an afternoon. The empty shops had been boarded up. A coat of paint will spruce up the hallway.

L.x: They're *doing up* (not *making up*) an old farmhouse in Wales.

L.p: You *clear out* a cupboard or a room when you remove the things you don't want, and you *throw out* old things. You *tidy away* things when you put them where they belong, and you *wipe down* surfaces with a cloth. In British English, you *hoover up* crumbs or dust.

L.e: I spent Saturday clearing out the garage. We threw out bags of old clothes. Tidy away your toys before bedtime. Wipe down the kitchen surfaces after cooking. Can you hoover up these crumbs?

L.p: You *settle in* when you start to feel at home somewhere new. You *put someone up* when they stay at your home, and you *put up with* noisy neighbours when you tolerate them. You *lock up* when you lock all the doors, and in winter pipes can *freeze up*.

L.e: It didn't take us long to settle in. My sister is putting me up for a week. I can't put up with the noise from next door. Don't forget to lock up before you go. The pipes froze up during the cold snap.

units.sub: dress up, slip on, smarten up

L.p: You *slip on* or *slip off* shoes or a jacket when you put them on or take them off quickly and easily. You *throw on* clothes when you put them on quickly and carelessly. You *do up* buttons and zips (fasten them), and you *change into* different clothes.

L.e: She slipped on her shoes and ran to the door. He slipped off his jacket and sat down. I threw on a jumper and went to answer the door. Do up your coat – it's freezing. I'll change into something more comfortable.

L.x: She *slipped on* (not *slid on*) her sandals and went out.

L.p: You *dress up* when you wear smart clothes and *dress down* when you wear casual ones. Informally, you *get dolled up* when you make yourself look very attractive. You *smarten up* when you make your appearance tidier, and people who are *dressed up to the nines* are wearing very smart, fashionable clothes.

L.e: We dressed up for the wedding. On Fridays staff can dress down. She spent an hour getting dolled up for the party. You need to smarten up before the interview. Everyone was dressed up to the nines.

L.h: C Altering and wearing out clothes

L.p: A tailor *lets out* clothes when making them wider and *takes in* clothes when making them narrower. You *take up* trousers when you make them shorter. Clothes *wear out* when they are used so much that they can't be worn, and children *grow out of* clothes when they become too big for them.

L.e: I've put on weight – these trousers need letting out. The jacket was too big, so I had it taken in. Could you take up these trousers by two centimetres? My jeans have worn out at the knees. The children grow out of their shoes so quickly.

units.sub: drift apart, settle down, make up

L.p: Informally, two people *hit it off* when they like each other immediately. You *fall for* someone when you fall in love with them. You *ask someone out* when you invite them on a date, and you *go out with* someone when you have a romantic relationship with them. Couples *get together* when their relationship starts.

L.e: We hit it off the moment we met. He fell for her at a friend's wedding. She finally asked him out after months of hints. They've been going out for a year. They got together at university.

L.x: They *got together* (not *got along together*) in their first year at university.

L.p: Couples *move in together* and may later *settle down* – start a stable life, often married. Informally, they *tie the knot* when they marry. Partners *stick by* each other in difficult times and *make up* after an argument.

L.e: They moved in together after six months. He's finally ready to settle down. They tied the knot in a small castle in Scotland. She stuck by him throughout his illness. We argued but made up the same evening.

L.p: People *fall out* when they argue and stop being friendly, and they *drift apart* when they gradually become less close. A couple *splits up* when their relationship ends, and one partner can *walk out on* the other. Informally, you *cheat on* a partner when you are unfaithful.

L.e: The two sisters fell out over the inheritance. We drifted apart after school. They split up after ten years together. He walked out on his family. She found out he'd been cheating on her.

units.sub: come across, bear up, mellow out

L.p: People *come across* as friendly, shy or arrogant – that is how they seem to others. You *take after* a relative when you resemble them. A talented person *stands out*, and you *put on* an accent or an act when you pretend. Someone *lives up to* their reputation when they are as good as people say.

L.e: She comes across as a bit cold, but she's very kind. He takes after his grandfather – they're both very stubborn. Her talent stood out from the start. He put on a posh accent for the interview. The new chef has lived up to his reputation.

L.x: He *put on* (not *wore*) a posh accent for the interview.

L.p: You *bear up* under pressure when you stay brave and cope. Informally, someone *goes to pieces* when they become unable to cope. People often *mellow out* (become calmer and more relaxed) as they get older, and they *grow out of* bad habits. A shy person *comes out of their shell* when they become more confident.

L.e: She's bearing up well since her husband died. He went to pieces when he heard the news. My father has mellowed out a lot in his old age. Most people grow out of their teenage moodiness. She came out of her shell at university.

L.p: Someone who *looks down on* others thinks they are better than them. People *show off* when they try to impress, and informally they *suck up to* someone powerful to gain an advantage. You *own up* when you admit a mistake, and you *stand up for* the things you believe in.

L.e: He looks down on anyone who didn't go to university. Stop showing off! He's always sucking up to the boss. She owned up to breaking the vase. My grandmother always stood up for the underdog.

units.sub: choke up, perk up, crack up

L.p: You *choke up* when you are so moved that you can hardly speak, and your eyes *well up* when tears come into them. You *break down* when you start crying uncontrollably. Informally, you *crack up* when you start laughing uncontrollably. Someone who *flares up* suddenly becomes angry.

L.e: He choked up when he tried to thank his parents. Her eyes welled up as the music started. She broke down when she heard the news. We cracked up when the dog stole his sandwich. He flares up at the slightest criticism.

L.x: He *choked up* (not *choked down*) when he tried to thank his parents.

L.p: Informally, you *perk up* when you become more cheerful and energetic, and your face *brightens up* when you look happier. You *simmer down* when you become calmer after being angry. A feeling *wears off* when it gradually disappears, and you *snap out of* a bad mood when you stop being unhappy (informal).

L.e: She perked up when she heard the good news. His face brightened up when he saw us. Simmer down – it's only a game. The excitement soon wore off. Come on, snap out of it! You've been miserable all week.

L.p: You *bottle up* feelings when you hide them, and you *hold back* tears when you stop yourself crying. You *open up* when you tell someone how you feel. You *take it out on* someone when you treat them badly because you are upset, and you *get* a worry *off your chest* when you finally talk about it.

L.e: It's not healthy to bottle up your anger. She held back her tears until she was alone. After a few weeks, he began to open up. Don't take it out on me! I'm glad I got that off my chest.

units.sub: drop round, tag along, live it up

L.p: Informally, you *drop round* or *pop round* (British English) when you visit someone's home without arranging it. You *have people over* when you invite them to your home, and a guest *stays over* when they spend the night. You *call in on* someone when you visit them on the way somewhere else.

L.e: Drop round any time – I'm usually in. Pop round for a coffee after work. We're having some friends over on Saturday. It's late – why don't you stay over? We called in on Grandma on our way home.

L.x: We *called in on* (not *called on in*) my aunt on the way home.

L.p: You *meet up* with friends and, informally, *hang out* together. You *tag along* when you go somewhere with a group, often without being invited. Informally, you *live it up* when you enjoy yourself in an exciting way, and you *paint the town red* when you go out to celebrate.

L.e: Let's meet up for lunch next week. We used to hang out at the skate park. Do you mind if I tag along? They're living it up in Ibiza. After the exams, we painted the town red.

L.p: Guests *turn up* at a party, or informally *show up*. A party *winds down* when it starts to end. Some guests *slip away* early without being noticed, while others *stay on* until the end.

L.e: Only half the people we invited turned up. He showed up two hours late. The party began to wind down around midnight. I slipped away before the speeches. A few guests stayed on to help clear up.

units.sub: come out in, flare up, keel over

L.p: You *come out in* spots or a rash when they suddenly appear on your skin, and you *break out in* a sweat. An old illness or injury *flares up* when it becomes worse again. You *black out* when you lose consciousness, and informally a person *keels over* when they fall to the ground because they are ill.

L.e: I came out in a rash after eating shellfish. He broke out in a cold sweat. My back problem has flared up again. She blacked out in the heat. An elderly man keeled over in the queue.

L.x: I *came out in* (not *came out with*) spots after eating nuts.

L.p: A doctor *checks you over* (examines you) and may *put you on* a medicine or a special diet. Your body *fights off* an infection, and the effects of a drug *wear off* after a time. Paramedics *bring* someone *round* when they make them conscious again.

L.e: The doctor checked me over and found nothing wrong. She's been put on antibiotics. My body managed to fight off the infection. The anaesthetic should wear off in an hour. The paramedics brought him round quickly.

L.p: You *get over* an illness when you recover from it, *shake off* a cold when you get rid of it and *pull through* a serious illness when you survive it. A doctor *signs you off* work when they say you are too ill to work, and later you *ease back into* work gradually.

L.e: It took me weeks to get over the virus. I can't seem to shake off this cough. Everyone was worried, but she pulled through. The doctor signed me off for a week. I'm easing back into work slowly.

units.sub: bulk up, slim down, double up

L.p: You *put on* weight when you get heavier and *slim down* when you lose weight. Informally, athletes *bulk up* when they become bigger and more muscular, and you *tone up* your muscles when you make them firmer. You *work off* calories when you use them through exercise.

L.e: I put on a few kilos over Christmas. She's slimmed down for her wedding. The boxer has bulked up for the fight. Swimming is a great way to tone up. I went for a run to work off lunch.

L.x: I *put on* (not *gained on*) weight over the holidays.

L.p: You *crouch down* when you bend your knees low, and you *stretch out* when you lie with your body straight. You *double up* when you bend forward suddenly in pain or laughter. You *breathe in* and breathe out, and you *come to* when you become conscious again.

L.e: She crouched down to look under the car. He stretched out on the sofa. We doubled up with laughter at his story. Breathe in slowly through your nose. He came to an hour later in hospital.

L.p: You *warm up* before exercise and *cool down* afterwards. You *cut out* foods when you stop eating them completely, and exercise *builds up* your stamina. A person *lets themselves go* when they stop caring about their health or appearance.

L.e: Always warm up properly before a run. Walk slowly for five minutes to cool down. I've cut out sugar completely. Running builds up your stamina. He let himself go after he retired.

units.sub: blurt out, babble on, rattle off

L.p: You *blurt out* something when you say it suddenly, without thinking – often something you should have kept secret. You *rattle off* or *reel off* a list when you say it quickly from memory. Informally, you *come out with* a surprising remark, and someone *pipes up* when they suddenly speak after being quiet.

L.e: He blurted out the news before I could stop him. She rattled off the names of all the capitals in Europe. The guide reeled off a list of dates. My nephew came out with a very rude word at dinner. A small voice at the back piped up: 'I know the answer!'

L.x: He *blurted out* (not *blurred out*) the secret before I could stop him.

L.p: Informally, someone who *babbles on* talks quickly and foolishly for a long time, and in British English someone who *rabbits on* talks about unimportant things. You *go on about* a subject when you talk about it too much, and you *harp on about* it when you keep mentioning it in an annoying way. A speaker *trails off* when their voice becomes quieter and stops.

L.e: He babbled on about his holiday for an hour. She's always rabbiting on about her diet. Please stop going on about the weather. My father keeps harping on about the war. Her voice trailed off as she realised her mistake.

L.p: You *speak up* when you speak louder, and you *speak out* when you say publicly what you think. You *cut in* when you interrupt, and informally you *chip in* when you add a comment. You *talk down to* someone when you speak to them as if they were stupid.

L.e: Speak up – we can't hear you at the back. She spoke out against the decision. Sorry to cut in, but your taxi's here. Several people chipped in with suggestions. I hate it when doctors talk down to me.

units.sub: edge along, creep up, dash off

L.p: Informally, you *dash off* when you leave in a hurry. A small animal *darts out* when it moves suddenly and quickly. You *race through* a task when you do it very fast. Informally, people *pile into* a car or a room when they get in quickly and untidily, and crowds *pour out* of a building when they leave in large numbers.

L.e: Sorry, I have to dash off – I'm late. A cat darted out in front of the car. We raced through the last part of the exam. Ten of us piled into the minibus. Crowds poured out of the stadium after the match.

L.x: Crowds *poured out* (not *poured off*) of the stadium after the match.

L.p: You *edge along* when you move slowly and carefully, a little at a time. You *creep up on* someone when you approach them quietly without being seen, and you *tiptoe out* of a room when you leave very quietly. Traffic *inches forward*, and someone who is old or tired *shuffles along* without lifting their feet.

L.e: We edged along the narrow ledge. She crept up on me and shouted 'Boo!' He tiptoed out so as not to wake the baby. The traffic inched forward. The old man shuffled along the corridor.

L.p: You *step aside* to let someone pass. Children *wander off* when they walk away without telling anyone. You *stroll along* when you walk slowly for pleasure, and informally you *head off* when you leave. You *double back* when you go back the way you came.

L.e: He stepped aside to let her pass. Don't wander off in the market – stay with me. We strolled along the seafront after dinner. We headed off early to beat the traffic. We realised we were lost and doubled back.
