units.sub: die off, spring up, branch out

L.p: In spring, plants *come up* (appear above the ground) and flowers *come out* (open). Weeds *spring up* everywhere when they appear suddenly. Many plants *die back* in winter – die above the ground but stay alive in their roots. Gardeners *cut back* bushes to make them smaller.

L.e: The first daffodils are coming up. The roses came out early this year. Weeds have sprung up all over the vegetable patch. The plants die back in winter and grow again in spring. Cut back the hedge in autumn.

L.x: In autumn, *cut back* (not *cut down*) the roses – don't kill them!

L.p: A species *dies out* when it disappears completely, while animals *die off* when large numbers of them die. A population *bounces back* when it recovers. A bird of prey *swoops down* on its victim, and informally an animal *holes up* when it hides somewhere for a long time.

L.e: The species died out thousands of years ago. Many fish died off during the heatwave. The otter population has bounced back. An eagle swooped down on the rabbit. The bear holes up in a cave for the winter.

L.p: Rivers *dry up* in a drought. Storms *wash away* sand, and over centuries the sea *wears away* rock and *eats into* the coastline. Mountains *tower over* the valleys beneath them.

L.e: Several rivers dried up during the drought. The storm washed away part of the beach. Over centuries, the sea has worn away the cliffs. Erosion is eating into the coast. The mountains tower over the village.

units.sub: ease off, set in, brighten up

L.p: Bad weather *sets in* when it begins and seems likely to last. The sky *clouds over*, a storm *blows up* (starts suddenly) and the wind *picks up* (becomes stronger). Fog *rolls in* from the sea.

L.e: Winter has set in early this year. It clouded over in the afternoon. A storm blew up while we were sailing. The wind picked up during the night. Thick fog rolled in from the sea.

L.x: The rain *set in* (not *set on*) after lunch and lasted all day.

L.p: Rain *eases off* when it becomes less, and informally it *lets up* when it stops. The weather *clears up* when it becomes fine. A storm *blows over* when it passes, and snow *melts away* in the spring sunshine.

L.e: The rain is finally easing off. It poured all day and didn't let up until evening. It should clear up by the afternoon. The storm blew over during the night. By March the snow had melted away.

L.p: Heavy snow *cuts off* villages, and lightning can *knock out* the power supply. In British English, a match is *rained off* when rain stops it. You *wrap up* warm in winter, and a car windscreen *ices up* on a freezing night.

L.e: The village was cut off for a week by snow. The storm knocked out the electricity. The match was rained off. Wrap up warm – it's minus five out there. The windscreen had iced up overnight.

units.sub: spread out, tuck away, open onto

L.p: A town *spreads out* along a river, and a big city *sprawls out* into the countryside (spreads in an untidy way). A flat *looks out over* a view, a room *opens onto* a garden or terrace, and a house *backs onto* a park when the park is behind it. A place that is *tucked away* is hidden or quiet.

L.e: The village spreads out along the river. The city sprawls out for miles in every direction. Our flat looks out over the harbour. The kitchen opens onto a small terrace. Their garden backs onto the river. There's a lovely café tucked away behind the church.

L.x: Our garden *backs onto* (not *backs on*) the river.

L.p: Old buildings are *done up* (renovated) or *knocked down* (demolished). New estates *spring up* on the edge of towns, and a town *grows up around* a market or a port. Informally, an area *goes downhill* when it gets worse.

L.e: The old cinema has been beautifully done up. They knocked down the mill to build flats. New housing estates are springing up everywhere. The town grew up around a busy port. The neighbourhood has gone downhill since the factory closed.

L.p: You *find your way around* a new place when you learn where things are, and you *get around* when you travel from place to place. You *stumble upon* a place when you find it by chance, and you *end up* somewhere you didn't plan to go. Streets *lead off* a square when they start from it.

L.e: It took me weeks to find my way around London. It's easy to get around by bus. We stumbled upon a tiny restaurant in the backstreets. We got lost and ended up at the station. Several narrow streets lead off the main square.

units.sub: pull out, pile up, set down

L.p: A car *pulls out* when it moves into the traffic, and a driver *pulls over* when they stop at the side of the road. Traffic *backs up* when it forms a long queue, and vehicles *pile up* when several crash into each other. A driver *cuts in* when they move suddenly in front of another car.

L.e: A van pulled out right in front of me. A police car signalled to us to pull over. Cars were backed up for three miles. Twenty vehicles piled up on the foggy motorway. A lorry cut in and nearly hit us.

L.x: A van *pulled out* (not *pulled off*) right in front of me.

L.p: In British English, buses *pick up* and *set down* passengers. You *flag down* a taxi when you wave to make it stop, and you *drop someone off* when you take them somewhere and leave them. A train *pulls in* when it arrives, and services *run late* when they are behind schedule.

L.e: The coach only sets down passengers at official stops. We flagged down a taxi outside the theatre. Could you drop me off at the station? The train pulled in ten minutes late. All services are running late because of the snow.

L.p: You *check in* at the airport, and friends may come to *see you off*. The plane *touches down* when it lands. Passengers *stop over* in a city during a long journey, and in British English you *meet someone off* a plane when you wait at the airport to collect them.

L.e: We checked in two hours before departure. My parents came to see me off. We touched down in Rome at noon. We stopped over in Singapore for two nights. I'll meet you off the plane.

units.sub: spark off, stand down, sweep through

L.p: News reports describe how a fire *sweeps through* a building (spreads quickly through it) and how violence *breaks out*. Protests *spring up* in many places at once, and an arrest can *spark off* riots. Later, the trouble *dies down*.

L.e: Fire swept through the warehouse in minutes. Violence broke out after the election results. Protests sprang up across the country. The arrest of the activist sparked off two nights of rioting. The row over the new law has died down.

L.x: The arrest *sparked off* (not *sparked up*) two nights of riots.

L.p: Politicians *stand down* when they resign, and governments are *voted out* at elections. A government *brings in* new laws. Ministers *play down* problems (make them seem less serious) and *talk up* their successes (make them seem greater).

L.e: The health minister stood down after the scandal. The government was voted out after twelve years. They're bringing in tougher laws on drink-driving. The minister played down the risks. The party talked up its record on jobs.

L.p: Journalists *follow up* a lead when they investigate further, and they *dig up* hidden information. Details *leak out*, and new facts *come to light* (become known). Other newspapers *pick up on* a story when they start reporting it too.

L.e: Reporters are following up reports of a second attack. A journalist dug up the minister's old emails. Details of the deal have leaked out. New evidence has come to light. Other papers quickly picked up on the story.

units.sub: cover up, hush up, own up

L.p: You *keep* something *back* when you don't reveal it. An organisation *covers up* a mistake or a crime when it hides it, and the attempt is *a cover-up*. Powerful people *hush up* a scandal (keep it secret). Companies *keep* new products *under wraps* until they are ready to launch them.

L.e: I felt she was keeping something back. The company tried to cover up the accident. There's been a cover-up at the highest level. The affair was hushed up for years. The new design is being kept under wraps until the launch.

L.x: The company tried to *cover up* (not *cover over*) the accident.

L.p: You *make up* a story when you invent it, and informally you *cook up* an excuse when you invent it dishonestly. You are *taken in* when someone deceives you, and you *fall for* a lie when you believe it. You *see through* a lie or a trick when you recognise that it is not true.

L.e: He made up a story about being robbed. She cooked up an excuse for missing the meeting. I was completely taken in by his charm. Don't fall for his promises. Fortunately, the bank saw through the scam.

L.p: Secrets *get out*, and informally you *let on* when you tell one. You *own up* when you admit the truth. Something *gives* you *away* when it reveals who you are or what you have done. Informally, investigators *ferret out* the truth when they find it after a long search.

L.e: Somehow the news got out. Please don't let on that I told you. He finally owned up to taking the money. Her nervous laugh gave her away. The reporters ferreted out the truth.

units.sub: crack down, bring in, clamp down

L.p: Governments *bring in* new laws (introduce them) and *lay down* rules (state them officially). Rules *apply to* the people they affect. Changes are sometimes *phased in* (introduced gradually), and an old law can be *done away with* (abolished).

L.e: The government is bringing in a ban on single-use plastics. The contract lays down strict conditions. The new rules apply to all members of staff. The changes will be phased in over two years. The old tax was done away with in 2015.

L.x: The new rules will be *phased in* (not *faded in*) over two years.

L.p: Authorities *crack down on* or *clamp down on* crime or bad behaviour when they act strongly to stop it. Judges *come down hard on* offenders when they punish them severely, and governments try to *stamp out* corruption. In formal English, people *abide by* rules (obey them). A police officer may *let* a driver *off* with a warning.

L.e: Police are cracking down on drivers who use mobile phones. The council is clamping down on illegal parking. Judges are coming down hard on online fraud. The new government promised to stamp out corruption. All visitors must abide by the safety rules. The officer let me off with a warning.

L.p: People *get away with* breaking rules when they are not punished, and they *get round* a rule when they find a legal way to avoid it. Officials sometimes *bend the rules* (break them a little). Anyone who *steps out of line* behaves badly, and the authorities *turn a blind eye* when they deliberately ignore wrongdoing.

L.e: He's been fiddling his expenses for years and getting away with it. Clever accountants help companies get round tax rules. Some officials were prepared to bend the rules. Anyone who steps out of line will be punished. The police seemed to turn a blind eye to the street drinking.

units.sub: boot up, back up, phase out

L.p: You *boot up* a computer when you start it, and you *shut* it *down* properly at the end of the day. You *plug in* a charger, *key in* information (type it) and *scroll down* a page on the screen.

L.e: My old laptop takes five minutes to boot up. Always shut down your computer properly. Plug in your phone before it runs out of battery. Key in your PIN and press Enter. Scroll down to the bottom of the page.

L.x: Always *shut down* (not *close down*) your laptop properly.

L.p: You *back up* your files when you make copies of them. Criminals *hack into* systems, and a virus can *wipe out* data (destroy it completely). You get *locked out* of an account after too many wrong passwords. Companies *roll out* updates when they release them to all users.

L.e: Back up your files every evening. A virus wiped out years of research. Someone hacked into my email account. I got locked out after three wrong passwords. The company is rolling out the update next week.

L.p: New technology *catches on* when it becomes popular, and old technology is *phased out*. You *trade in* an old phone when you give it as part of the payment for a new one. A network *goes down* when it stops working, and it can be hard to *keep up with* every new development.

L.e: Smart speakers caught on very quickly. The bank is phasing out its paper statements. I traded in my old phone for a discount. The whole network went down for two hours. It's hard to keep up with all the changes.

units.sub: tuck in, knock back, wash down

L.p: In informal British English you *tuck in*, and in general informal English you *dig in*, when you start eating with enthusiasm. Informally, you *wolf down* food when you eat it very quickly and *pig out* when you eat far too much. You *pick at* your food when you eat only a little because you are not hungry.

L.e: The food's on the table – tuck in! Dig in, everyone, before it gets cold. He wolfed down his lunch in five minutes. She just picked at her salad. We pigged out on chocolate at Christmas.

L.x: Dinner's ready – *dig in* (not *dig up*)!

L.p: Informally, you *knock back* a drink when you drink it quickly, and you *wash down* food with a drink. You *top up* someone's glass when you fill it again. A person *sobers up* when they stop being drunk, and you *cut down on* coffee or alcohol when you drink less of it.

L.e: He knocked back his coffee and ran for the train. We had sandwiches washed down with lemonade. Can I top up your glass? Have some water and sober up before you go home. I've cut down on caffeine.

L.p: Informally, you *rustle up* something to eat from whatever is available, and in British English you *knock up* a quick meal. A sauce *boils down* when it becomes thicker as water evaporates. You *dish up* food when you serve it, and food *goes off* when it becomes bad.

L.e: I'll rustle up something for lunch. Give me ten minutes and I'll knock up a sandwich. Let the sauce boil down until it's thick. Dad dished up the roast. This yoghurt has gone off.

units.sub: come by, come up against, come into

L.p: You *come by* something when you get it, especially something hard to find: *Good jobs are hard to come by*. You *come into* money when you inherit it, and you *come across* something when you find it by chance. An opportunity *comes up* when it appears, and you *come up with* an idea or a sum of money when you produce it.

L.e: Cheap flats are hard to come by in London. She came into a fortune when her uncle died. I came across some old letters in the attic. A job has come up in the sales team. We need to come up with £5,000 by Friday.

L.x: Good jobs are hard to *come by* (not *come for*) round here.

L.p: You *come up against* difficulties or opposition when you have to deal with them, and you *come in for* criticism when you receive it. A problem *comes to a head* when it reaches a crisis. A plan *comes apart* when it fails, and you *come through* a difficult time when you survive it.

L.e: The project came up against strong local opposition. The referee came in for a lot of criticism. Things came to a head at the annual meeting. Their plans came apart when the funding was withdrawn. She came through the operation well.

L.p: You *come round to* an idea when you start to accept it, and a committee *comes down on* one side when it decides to support it. People *come out against* a plan when they publicly oppose it. A result *comes down to* one factor when it depends mainly on it, and something *comes about* when it happens.

L.e: He eventually came round to the idea of moving. The committee came down on the side of the residents. Several MPs have come out against the plan. In the end, it all comes down to money. How did the mistake come about?

units.sub: get across, get round to, get by

L.p: You *get across* an idea when you make people understand it, and something *gets through to* someone when they finally understand it. You *get at* something when you try to express it (*What are you getting at?*), and informally you *get at* someone when you keep criticising them. You *get round* someone when you persuade them by being charming.

L.e: She's very good at getting her message across. I tried to warn him, but nothing seemed to get through to him. I don't understand – what are you getting at? Stop getting at me! She always knows how to get round her father.

L.x: He's good at *getting* his ideas *across* (not *getting* his ideas *over to*).

L.p: You *get by* when you manage with difficulty, and you *get through* a hard time or a lot of work. You *get round to* something when you finally find time to do it. You *get out of* a duty when you avoid it, and you *get away with* something wrong when you are not punished. You *get over* a shock or an illness when you recover.

L.e: We get by on one income. I don't know how we got through that winter. I'll get round to fixing the gate one day. He always manages to get out of the washing-up. She cheated and got away with it. It took her years to get over the shock.

L.p: You *get ahead* when you succeed in your career, and you *get on* in life. Informally, you *get on to* someone when you contact them about a problem. You *get down to* work when you start it seriously, and you *get together* with friends when you meet socially. Something *gets you down* when it makes you unhappy.

L.e: You need qualifications to get ahead these days. I'll get on to the council about the broken streetlight. It's time to get down to some serious revision. Let's get together over the holidays. The endless rain is getting me down.

units.sub: go about, go under, go in for

L.p: You *go about* a task in a particular way (*How do I go about getting a visa?*). You *go in for* an activity when you like doing it regularly, or when you enter a competition. You *go into* a subject when you discuss it in detail, and you *go over* something when you check it. You *go through* with a plan when you do it although it is difficult.

L.e: How should I go about finding a good lawyer? I don't really go in for team sports. She's going in for the poetry competition. I won't go into the details now. Let's go over the figures again. In the end, he couldn't go through with the wedding.

L.x: How do I *go about* (not *go around*) applying for a visa?

L.p: A business *goes under* when it fails. Prices *go down*, food *goes off*, and a situation *goes downhill* when it gets worse. A plan *goes wrong* or *goes awry* (formal), and a joke *goes down badly* when people don't like it. A person *goes to pieces* when they can't cope.

L.e: Hundreds of shops went under during the recession. Since the new owners arrived, the pub has gone downhill. All our plans went awry. His comments went down badly with the audience. He went to pieces in the final.

L.p: You *go along with* a plan or person when you agree, often unwillingly, and you *go back on* a promise when you break it. You *go on* when you continue, and you *go on about* something when you talk about it too much. Two things *go together* when they suit each other, and you *go for* something when you choose it or try to get it.

L.e: I went along with the plan to avoid an argument. The government has gone back on its promise. Please go on – I'm listening. He's always going on about his car. Red wine and cheese go together perfectly. I'll go for the fish, please.

units.sub: keep at, keep up with, keep to

L.p: You *keep at* something when you continue working hard at it, and you *keep on* doing something when you continue, often annoyingly. You *keep up* a good standard (continue it), and you *keep up with* people or changes when you stay at the same level. You *keep going* when you continue despite difficulties.

L.e: Learning a language is hard, but keep at it. He keeps on interrupting me. Keep up the good work! It's hard to keep up with the latest technology. My legs were aching, but I kept going.

L.x: Learning Chinese is hard, but *keep at it* (not *keep on it*).

L.p: You *keep to* rules, a plan or a path when you follow them, and you *keep to the point* when you don't talk about other subjects. You *keep down* costs or noise (keep them low) and *keep back* information (don't reveal it). You *keep* something *up* when you continue it, and you *keep your head down* when you avoid attention.

L.e: Please keep to the footpath. Try to keep to the point in your essay. We need to keep costs down. I felt he was keeping something back. Keep your head down until the fuss blows over.

L.p: You *keep away from* someone or something dangerous, and you *keep off* grass, a subject or a food (avoid it). You *keep out of* trouble or an argument (avoid getting involved), and you *keep* something *from* someone when you don't tell them. You *keep in with* someone (British English) when you stay friendly with them because they are useful.

L.e: Keep away from the edge of the platform. Please keep off the grass. Let's keep off the subject of politics. Try to keep out of trouble. They kept the news from their children. He keeps in with the boss.

units.sub: take aback, take in, take to

L.p: You are *taken aback* when something surprises or shocks you. You are *taken in* when someone deceives you. Something *takes you back* when it makes you remember the past. You *take* something *in* when you understand and remember it, and you *take in* the sights when you look at them carefully.

L.e: I was taken aback by her rudeness. Don't be taken in by his charm. That song really takes me back. There was too much information to take in. We spent the afternoon taking in the sights.

L.x: I was *taken aback* (not *taken back*) by her rudeness.

L.p: You *take to* someone or something when you start to like them, and you *take to* doing something when you start doing it as a habit. You *take up* a hobby (start it) and *take on* work or responsibility (accept it). A company *takes on* staff, and one company *takes over* another.

L.e: The children took to their new teacher immediately. He's taken to going for long walks. I took up the cello at sixty. She's taken on too much work. The hotel is taking on extra staff for the summer. The firm was taken over last year.

L.p: You *take back* something you said when you admit it was wrong. You *take* something *out on* someone when you treat them badly because you are upset. You *take off* someone when you copy them to make people laugh, and a product *takes off* when it becomes popular. You *take apart* a machine, and you *take down* notes or a structure.

L.e: I take back what I said – I was wrong. Don't take it out on me – it's not my fault. She takes off the headteacher brilliantly. The app really took off last year. He took the engine apart to find the problem. They took down the tents after the festival.
